column2: The citric acid cycle takes place in the {{c1::mitochondrial matrix}}.
The citric acid cycle oxidizes {{c1::acetyl-CoA}} to CO₂ and transfers electrons to carriers used by the ETC.
Each turn of the TCA cycle makes one {{c1::ATP or GTP}} via substrate-level phosphorylation (not via the ETC).
In the citric acid cycle, GTP/ATP is made by substrate-level phosphorylation during the conversion of {{c1::succinyl-CoA to succinate}}.
High {{c1::ADP}} signals low ATP and increases catabolic flux through key enzymes.
Acetyl-CoA joins {{c1::oxaloacetate}} to form {{c1::citrate}} at the start of each cycle turn.
Per turn, the citric acid cycle releases {{c1::2}} CO₂ and makes {{c1::3}} NADH.
When ADP is high, why do metabolic pathways generally speed up?
column3: Allosteric activation of rate-limiting enzymes — the cell needs to regenerate ATP.

column2: Why does the citric acid cycle itself produce little ATP directly?
column3: Most of its energy is captured as NADH and FADH₂, which feed the electron transport chain — where the bulk of ATP is actually made.

column2: Enzymes speed a reaction by lowering its {{c1::activation energy}}, without changing {{c1::ΔG}}.
ΔG > 0 → {{c1::endergonic}}; ΔG < 0 → {{c1::exergonic}}.
Reaction rate depends on {{c1::activation energy}}, not ΔG.
{{c1::Competitive}} inhibitors bind the active site; allosteric inhibitors bind {{c1::elsewhere}} and change enzyme shape/activity.
An enzyme reaches {{c1::Vmax}} when its active sites are {{c1::saturated}} with substrate.
Why compare reaction rates (not ΔG) to judge activation energy?
column3: ΔG reflects spontaneity/energy change; Ea sets the barrier that controls rate at a given temperature.

column2: How does an allosteric inhibitor differ from a competitive inhibitor?
column3: Competitive: active site, blocks substrate. Allosteric: non-active site, conformation change (often lowers affinity).

column2: The {{c1::active site}} is the region of an enzyme where substrate binds and catalysis occurs.
Induced fit: when substrate binds, the enzyme's {{c1::active site}} changes shape to fit it more snugly.
Heating an enzyme far above its optimum {{c1::denatures}} it, lowering its activity.
Glycolysis takes place in the {{c1::cytoplasm}} (cytosol), not the mitochondrion.
Net ATP yield of glycolysis per glucose is {{c1::2}} (4 produced − 2 invested).
Glycolysis reduces NAD⁺ to {{c1::NADH}} and ends in two molecules of {{c1::pyruvate}}.
The committed, rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis is {{c1::phosphofructokinase-1}} (PFK-1).
Under anaerobic conditions in muscle, what happens to pyruvate and why?
column3: It is reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD⁺, so glycolysis (and ATP output) can continue.

column2: The plasma membrane's core structure is the {{c1::phospholipid bilayer}}.
In a phospholipid, the phosphate head is {{c1::hydrophilic}} and the fatty-acid tails are {{c1::hydrophobic}}.
{{c1::Active}} transport moves solutes against their gradient (needs energy); {{c1::passive}} transport moves them down the gradient.
Osmosis is the diffusion of {{c1::water}} across a selectively permeable membrane.
Why can O₂ cross the membrane by simple diffusion but glucose usually cannot?
column3: O₂ is small and nonpolar, so it dissolves through the lipid bilayer; glucose is larger and polar, so it needs a transport protein.

column2: Cholesterol in animal cell membranes modulates membrane {{c1::fluidity}}.
DNA replication is {{c1::semiconservative}}: each daughter has one old and one new strand.
In DNA, A pairs with {{c1::T}} and G pairs with {{c1::C}}.
The two strands of DNA run {{c1::antiparallel}} and are complementary.
{{c1::Helicase}} unwinds the double helix; {{c1::ligase}} joins Okazaki fragments.
Why is the lagging strand synthesized in fragments?
column3: DNA polymerase only builds 5'→3'; on the lagging strand the template runs the opposite way, so it is copied in short Okazaki fragments.

column2: DNA polymerase builds new strands only in the {{c1::5'→3'}} direction.
A monohybrid cross Aa × Aa gives a phenotypic ratio of {{c1::3:1}} and a genotypic ratio of {{c1::1:2:1}}.
{{c1::Genotype}} is the genetic makeup; {{c1::phenotype}} is the observable trait.
Mendel's law of {{c1::segregation}}: the two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation.
A testcross uses a {{c1::homozygous recessive}} partner to reveal an unknown genotype.
In codominance, how is the heterozygote expressed?
column3: Both alleles are expressed fully and at the same time (e.g., type AB blood) — not blended.

column2: Genes far apart on the same chromosome assort nearly {{c1::independently}} because of crossing over.
Brønsted–Lowry acids {{c1::donate}} H⁺; bases {{c1::accept}} H⁺.
CH₃COOH is a {{c1::weaker}} acid than HCl (conjugate base strength runs opposite to acid strength).
When product is added to a reaction at equilibrium, the reaction shifts toward {{c1::reactants}}.
Increasing {{c1::[H⁺]}} shifts a base toward its {{c1::protonated}} (conjugate acid) form.
HF and HCN in water: the ionization equilibrium lies to the {{c1::left}}, so both are {{c1::weak}} acids (only partial ionization).
A buffer contains a {{c1::weak acid}} and its {{c1::conjugate base}}, so it resists pH change.
At 25 °C a neutral solution has [H⁺] = {{c1::1×10⁻⁷ M}} and pH = {{c1::7}}.
Why is the conjugate base of a strong acid a very weak base?
column3: A strong acid gives up its proton almost completely because the resulting conjugate base is stable and has little tendency to reaccept H⁺.

column2: For a strong acid, pH = −log[H⁺]; a 0.010 M HCl solution has pH {{c1::2}}.
A conjugate acid–base pair differs by one H⁺, e.g. {{c1::H₂CO₃}} / {{c1::HCO₃⁻}}.
Each pH unit is a 10× change in [H⁺], so pH 4 is {{c1::100}}× more acidic than pH 6.
In a galvanic cell, oxidation occurs at the {{c1::anode}} and reduction at the {{c1::cathode}}.
A galvanic cell has a {{c1::positive}} E°cell, so its redox reaction is {{c1::spontaneous}} (ΔG° < 0).
The {{c1::salt bridge}} keeps the half-cells electrically neutral by allowing ion flow.
How does electrolysis differ from a galvanic cell in energy terms?
column3: Electrolysis uses external electrical energy to drive a nonspontaneous reaction; a galvanic cell releases energy from a spontaneous one.

column2: The species that is oxidized is the {{c1::reducing agent}} (e.g., Zn in Zn + Cu²⁺).
By the Nernst equation, raising the concentration of product ions {{c1::lowers}} the cell potential.
Gibbs free energy: ΔG = ΔH − {{c1::T}}ΔS.
A reaction is spontaneous at all temperatures when ΔH is {{c1::negative}} and ΔS is {{c1::positive}}.
At equilibrium, ΔG = {{c1::0}}.
Entropy (S) measures the {{c1::disorder}} (dispersal of energy and matter) of a system.
Does a negative ΔG mean the reaction is fast?
column3: No — ΔG < 0 means spontaneous (thermodynamically favorable). Speed is set separately by activation energy / kinetics.

column2: When ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0, a reaction is spontaneous only at {{c1::high}} temperature.
A spontaneous process proceeds without a continuous {{c1::external energy}} input.
A catalyst lowers the {{c1::activation energy}}; it does not change {{c1::ΔG}} or the equilibrium.
Raising temperature speeds a reaction because more molecules exceed the {{c1::activation energy}}.
For rate = k[A][B]², the overall reaction order is {{c1::3}}.
Why doesn't a catalyst change the equilibrium position?
column3: It lowers activation energy for the forward and reverse steps equally, speeding both — so it changes rate, not the equilibrium constant.

column2: The rate constant k depends on {{c1::temperature}} and a {{c1::catalyst}}, not on reactant concentration.
For a reaction first order in A, doubling [A] multiplies the rate by {{c1::2}}.
A {{c1::zero-order}} reaction's rate is independent of reactant concentration.
Activation energy is the {{c1::minimum}} energy reactants need in order to react.
Continuity for an incompressible fluid: A₁v₁ = {{c1::A₂v₂}} (volume flow rate is conserved).
By Bernoulli's principle, where fluid speed is higher, pressure is {{c1::lower}} (at constant height).
An object floats when the buoyant force equals its {{c1::weight}}.
In a pipe that narrows, what happens to the fluid's speed and why?
column3: Speed increases: the same volume per second must pass through a smaller cross-sectional area (continuity).

column2: {{c1::Pascal's}} principle: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout it.
The SI unit of pressure, the pascal, equals {{c1::N/m²}}.
Encoding gets information in; {{c1::storage}} holds it; {{c1::retrieval}} gets it back out.
Short-term (working) memory holds about {{c1::7 ± 2}} items.
{{c1::Long-term}} memory is the relatively permanent, large-capacity store.
The {{c1::serial position}} effect: the first and last list items are recalled best.
What is the difference between explicit and implicit memory?
column3: Explicit (declarative): consciously recalled facts and events. Implicit: skills and conditioned responses expressed without conscious recall.

column2: Maintaining information in short-term memory by repetition is {{c1::rehearsal}}.
{{c1::Context-dependent}} memory: recall improves when the retrieval context matches encoding.
In Pavlov's dogs, food is the {{c1::unconditioned stimulus}} and salivation to food is the {{c1::unconditioned response}}.
After conditioning, the bell becomes the {{c1::conditioned stimulus}}.
A reinforcer {{c1::increases}} a behavior; a punisher {{c1::decreases}} it.
Negative reinforcement {{c1::increases}} behavior by {{c1::removing}} an aversive stimulus.
How does extinction occur in classical conditioning?
column3: Presenting the conditioned stimulus repeatedly without the unconditioned stimulus weakens and eventually eliminates the conditioned response.

column2: A {{c1::variable-ratio}} schedule reinforces behavior after an unpredictable number of responses.
The {{c1::fundamental attribution error}}: we over-credit others' behavior to personality and under-weight the situation.
{{c1::Conformity}} is matching a group standard; {{c1::obedience}} is following an authority's command.
The {{c1::bystander}} effect: the more people present, the less likely any one person helps.
{{c1::Cognitive dissonance}} is the discomfort from holding conflicting attitudes or acting against one's attitude.
What did Milgram's obedience studies demonstrate?
column3: Ordinary people will often follow an authority figure's instructions to harm another — the power of obedience to authority.

column2: An {{c1::attitude}} is an evaluation (favorable or unfavorable) of a person, object, or idea.
Health {{c1::disparities}} are preventable differences in health outcomes across social groups.
The social {{c1::gradient}} in health: outcomes tend to improve with higher socioeconomic status.
SES is commonly measured by income, education, and {{c1::occupation}}.
What is a social determinant of health? Give an example.
column3: A non-medical social factor that shapes health — e.g., access to education, income level, or safe housing.

column2: A competitive inhibitor binds the enzyme's {{c1::active site}}, directly competing with substrate for binding.
Noncompetitive inhibition: Vmax {{c1::decreases}} while Km stays {{c1::unchanged}}.
Km is the substrate concentration at {{c1::half of Vmax}}; a higher Km means lower substrate affinity.
In an enzyme assay comparing 'with inhibitor' vs 'without', which variable is held constant and which is deliberately varied?
column3: Hold the total enzyme amount (and temperature) constant. Substrate concentration is the independent variable you vary; reaction velocity is the dependent variable you measure.

column2: How does Km differ in kind from Keq?
column3: Km is a kinetic quantity — the [S] at half-Vmax, describing how the enzyme handles substrate. Keq is a thermodynamic quantity — the equilibrium ratio set by the free-energy difference between reactants and products.

column2: A competitive inhibitor raises the enzyme's {{c1::apparent Km}} (more substrate is needed to reach a given velocity) because it competes for the active site.
Uncompetitive inhibition lowers {{c1::both}} Vmax and Km, because the inhibitor binds only the enzyme–substrate complex.
Competitive inhibition is {{c1::surmountable}}: the inhibitor binds reversibly at the active site, so adding excess substrate outcompetes it.
E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode); the half-cell with the {{c1::higher (more positive)}} reduction potential is the cathode.
ΔG° = {{c1::−nFE°cell}}, so a positive E°cell gives a {{c1::negative}} ΔG° (spontaneous).
For ΔG° = −nFE°cell, what is n?
column3: n is the number of moles of electrons transferred in the balanced redox reaction (e.g., n = 2 for Zn(s) + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu(s)).

column2: Ecell (the actual potential) changes with ion concentrations via the Nernst equation, but E°cell (standard) is {{c1::fixed}}.
A galvanic cell keeps doing electrical work until it reaches {{c1::equilibrium}}, at which point Ecell = {{c1::0}} (a dead battery).
Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]); when [A⁻] = [HA], pH = {{c1::pKa}}.
In a buffer, which species neutralizes a small amount of added strong acid (H⁺), and what does it become?
column3: The conjugate base (A⁻) reacts with the added H⁺ and is converted into the weak acid (HA), consuming the added acid.

column2: If something suppresses a weak acid's dissociation, what happens to [H⁺] and pH?
column3: Less dissociation releases fewer H⁺, so [H⁺] falls and the pH rises.

column2: A strong acid ionizes {{c1::completely}} (lower pH); a weak acid at equal concentration ionizes only {{c1::partially}} (higher pH).
For independent genes, the probability of a combined genotype/phenotype is the {{c1::product}} of the separate gene probabilities (e.g., 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/6).
A dihybrid cross of two double heterozygotes (YyRr × YyRr) gives a phenotypic ratio of {{c1::9:3:3:1}} under independent assortment.
In a testcross (× homozygous recessive), how do you read one gene's result?
column3: A ~1:1 dominant:recessive split means the tested parent is heterozygous for that gene; offspring that are all dominant mean it is homozygous dominant.

column2: One glucose → 2 pyruvate → 2 acetyl-CoA → {{c1::2}} turns of the citric acid cycle.
Which stages of glucose oxidation make ATP/GTP by substrate-level phosphorylation, and which supplies the much larger remainder?
column3: Glycolysis and the citric acid cycle make ATP/GTP directly by substrate-level phosphorylation; the electron transport chain (oxidative phosphorylation) supplies the much larger remainder.

column2: In osmosis, water moves toward the {{c1::hypertonic}} (higher-solute) side; a cell in a hypotonic solution {{c1::swells}} and may lyse.
To write the complement of a DNA strand in the 5'→3' direction, what two steps do you take?
column3: Pair each base (A-T, G-C), then reverse the order — because the two strands are antiparallel (e.g., 5'-AATGC-3' → 5'-GCATT-3').

column2: When combining ΔH (in kJ) with ΔS (in J) in ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, first convert both to the {{c1::same energy unit}} (e.g., kJ → J).
In a rate law rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, the exponent on each reactant is its {{c1::order}}; the sum m+n is the overall order.
A {{c1::variable-ratio}} schedule (e.g., gambling) produces a high, steady response rate that is highly resistant to extinction.
How is negative reinforcement different from punishment?
column3: Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus and thereby increases a behavior; punishment (positive or negative) decreases a behavior.

column2: {{c1::Actor–observer}} bias: we attribute our own behavior to the situation but others' behavior to their disposition (the latter overlaps the fundamental attribution error).
How does a social gradient in health differ from a simple poverty threshold?
column3: A gradient means health improves at every step up the SES ladder — not only the poorest are worse off. A threshold would mean only those below a cutoff suffer.

column2: An {{c1::endergonic}} reaction absorbs (consumes) energy; an {{c1::exergonic}} reaction releases energy.
Both endergonic and exergonic reactions must first overcome an {{c1::activation-energy}} barrier before they proceed.
Activation energy is a {{c1::kinetic}} property, so it cannot be inferred from ΔG or spontaneity (which are {{c1::thermodynamic}}).
An allosteric {{c1::activator}} raises, while an allosteric {{c1::inhibitor}} lowers, the active site's affinity for substrate.
The {{c1::allosteric}} site is a regulatory binding site separate from the active site.
An enzyme is a catalyst, so it is {{c1::not consumed}} by the reaction it speeds up.
During catalysis the substrate is {{c1::chemically transformed}} into product (it is not left unchanged).
{{c1::Denaturation}} is the loss of a protein's 3-D shape, which distorts the enzyme's active site and lowers activity.
A {{c1::controlled}} variable is held constant so any change in the outcome can be attributed to the treatment.
In an experiment the {{c1::independent}} variable is deliberately changed and the {{c1::dependent}} variable is measured.
ΔG and Keq depend only on the {{c1::free-energy difference}} between reactants and products, which a catalyst or inhibitor cannot change.
Ammonia is a weak base: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ {{c1::NH₄⁺}} + {{c1::OH⁻}}.
Common-ion effect: adding an ion already in the equilibrium (e.g., NH₄⁺ to NH₃, or acetate to acetic acid) {{c1::suppresses}} the weak acid/base ionization.
The {{c1::weaker}} the acid, the stronger its conjugate base (and the reverse).
A strong acid and strong base cannot form a buffer — they simply {{c1::react to completion}}.
At 25 °C the water autoionization constant Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = {{c1::1.0×10⁻¹⁴}}.
A neutral aqueous solution is defined by {{c1::[H⁺] = [OH⁻]}}.
By Henderson–Hasselbalch, raising pH by 1 unit above the pKa multiplies the [A⁻]/[HA] ratio by {{c1::10}}.
Suppressing a weak acid's ionization lowers its {{c1::percent dissociation}}.
Raising temperature increases reaction rate but does {{c1::not}} lower the activation energy or change ΔG.
The temperature dependence of the rate constant k is described by the {{c1::Arrhenius}} equation.
Activation energy is the barrier to reach the {{c1::transition state}}; it is not the reactant–product energy difference (ΔH/ΔG).
Method of initial rates: find a reactant's order by comparing experiments in which only {{c1::that reactant's}} concentration changes.
Thermodynamic favorability (ΔG) and reaction rate are {{c1::independent}} — a spontaneous reaction can still be very slow.
